title: There's a Species of Ant That Can Build Living Bridges
fact: Army ants link their bodies together to form temporary bridges and rafts, allowing entire colonies to cross gaps or float across water using collective self-assembly.

title: The First Photograph of a Human Being Was an Accident
fact: Louis Daguerre's 1838 photo of a Paris street appears empty except for a man getting his shoes shined, who stood still long enough to be captured by the camera's long exposure time while everyone else moving was rendered invisible.

title: Some Volcanoes Erupt Blue Flames Instead of Red Lava
fact: Indonesia's Kawah Ijen volcano is known for its electric-blue flames, caused by sulfuric gases igniting upon contact with air rather than the glow of molten rock itself.

title: The Inventor of the Ballpoint Pen's Name Became a Word for Pen in Several Languages
fact: László Bíró, the Hungarian-Argentine inventor of the modern ballpoint pen, is honored in countries like Argentina, where pens are informally called 'birome' after him.

title: There's a Lake That Turns Animals into Statues
fact: Tanzania's Lake Natron has such high alkalinity that it calcifies the bodies of animals that die in its waters, preserving them in eerily lifelike, statue-like poses.

title: The Great Fire of London Killed Surprisingly Few People
fact: Despite destroying over 13,000 houses in 1666, official records list only a handful of deaths, though historians suspect the true toll among the poor went undocumented.

title: Cats Can't Taste Sweetness
fact: Domestic cats lack the functional taste receptor gene for sweetness, meaning they are biologically unable to perceive sugary flavors the way humans and many other animals can.

title: There's a Number So Large It's Called a Googolplex
fact: A googolplex is 10 raised to the power of a googol (10^100), a number so vast that writing out all its digits would require more space than exists in the observable universe.

title: The World's Oldest Living Organism Is a Fungus in Oregon
fact: A honey fungus (Armillaria ostoyae) in Oregon's Malheur National Forest spans nearly 2,400 acres underground and is estimated to be at least 2,400 years old.

title: Ketchup Was Once Sold as Medicine
fact: In the 1830s, an Ohio physician marketed tomato-based ketchup pills as a cure for indigestion, jaundice, and diarrhea, though the claims were later debunked.

title: There's a Bird That Can Sleep While Flying
fact: Alpine swifts have been recorded staying airborne for over six months at a time, using brief periods of unihemispheric sleep to rest one half of their brain while continuing to fly.

title: The Amazon Rainforest Produces Its Own Rain
fact: Through a process called evapotranspiration, the Amazon releases enormous amounts of water vapor from its trees, generating rain clouds that sustain much of the region's own rainfall cycle.

title: A Piece of Paper Can't Be Folded in Half More Than a Certain Number of Times
fact: Due to the exponential growth in thickness, a standard sheet of paper can typically only be folded in half about 7 to 8 times by hand before it becomes physically impossible to fold further.

title: There Was a 'Great Moon Hoax' That Fooled 19th-Century Readers
fact: In 1835, the New York Sun published a series of fake articles claiming astronomers had discovered bat-like humanoids and unicorns living on the Moon, and the hoax was widely believed for weeks.

title: Kangaroos Can't Walk Backwards
fact: The structure of a kangaroo's legs and its large tail make it anatomically incapable of moving backwards, which is why the animal appears on Australia's coat of arms as a symbol of forward progress.

title: There's a Town in Norway Where the Sun Doesn't Set for Months
fact: Located above the Arctic Circle, the town of Svalbard experiences continuous daylight from around late April to late August due to Earth's axial tilt.

title: The First Recorded Use of a Zero as a Number Came from Ancient India
fact: Mathematicians in India, notably Brahmagupta in the 7th century CE, were among the first to treat zero as a number in its own right with defined arithmetic rules, rather than just a placeholder.

title: Some Species of Turtles Breathe Through Their Butts
fact: Certain freshwater turtles, like the Fitzroy River turtle, can absorb oxygen from water through specialized tissue in their cloaca, allowing them to stay submerged for extended periods.

title: There's a Forest in Poland Where All the Trees Bend the Same Way
fact: The Crooked Forest near Gryfino, Poland, contains around 400 pine trees with trunks bent sharply northward at the base, a phenomenon whose cause remains a mystery to researchers.

title: The Inventor of the Modern Umbrella Faced Public Ridicule
fact: When Jonas Hanway popularized carrying an umbrella in 18th-century London, he was mocked and even pelted by coachmen who feared the invention would hurt their rain-related business.

title: A Colony of Bees Can Recognize Human Faces
fact: Studies have shown honeybees can be trained to distinguish between different human faces using a technique called configural processing, similar to how humans recognize faces.

title: There's a Nuclear Bomb Still Lost in the Ocean Off Georgia's Coast
fact: In 1958, a U.S. Air Force bomber accidentally dropped a hydrogen bomb into the waters near Tybee Island, Georgia, during a training mishap, and it has never been recovered.

title: The Human Eye Can Detect a Single Photon of Light
fact: Research published in Nature Communications in 2016 demonstrated that under controlled conditions, human observers could reliably sense the arrival of just one photon.

title: There's a Species of Shrimp That Can Change Its Sex
fact: Many species of cleaner shrimp and other crustaceans are protandric hermaphrodites, starting life as males and later transitioning into females as they mature.

title: The Sound Barrier Was Once Thought to Be an Impenetrable Wall
fact: Before Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in 1947, many engineers believed aircraft approaching that speed would be torn apart by an invisible physical 'wall,' a myth largely dispelled by his successful flight.

title: There's a River in Colombia Known as the 'River of Five Colors'
fact: Caño Cristales turns vivid shades of red, yellow, green, blue, and black during a specific seasonal window, caused by a unique aquatic plant called Macarenia clavigera reacting to sunlight levels.

title: The First Vending Machines in America Sold Chewing Gum on Subway Platforms
fact: In 1888, the Adams Gum Company installed vending machines on New York City elevated train platforms, marking one of the earliest commercial vending machine uses in the United States.

title: There's a Species of Spider That Builds Fake Decoy Spiders in Its Web
fact: Certain orb-weaving spiders in the Amazon construct larger-than-life decoy spiders out of leaves, debris, and silk to confuse or intimidate potential predators.

title: Antarctica Has a Waterfall That Runs Blood Red
fact: Blood Falls, at the tip of Taylor Glacier, gets its striking red color from iron-rich saltwater seeping out of a subglacial lake and oxidizing on contact with air.

title: There Was a Point When More People Were Born in China Than Existed in the Roman Empire
fact: At the height of the Han Dynasty around 2 CE, China's population is estimated to have exceeded 55 million, roughly comparable to or exceeding contemporary Roman Empire population estimates.

title: Some Caterpillars Can Whistle to Scare Off Predators
fact: The walnut sphinx caterpillar forces air out of tiny holes along its body called spiracles, producing a whistling sound loud enough to startle birds into dropping it.

title: There's a City Built Entirely Underground in Australia
fact: The opal-mining town of Coober Pedy has residents living in underground dugout homes to escape scorching desert surface temperatures that can exceed 50 degrees Celsius.

title: A Massive Ice Age Once Turned Nearly the Entire Earth into a Giant Snowball
fact: Geological evidence suggests that around 650 to 700 million years ago, Earth may have been almost entirely covered in ice in an event scientists call 'Snowball Earth.'

title: There's a Species of Wasp That Turns Cockroaches into Zombie Slaves
fact: The emerald jewel wasp stings a cockroach's brain with venom that suppresses its escape reflex, then leads it by an antenna to its burrow to serve as living food for its larvae.

title: The Longest Total Solar Eclipse of the 21st Century Will Last Over 7 Minutes
fact: On July 16, 2186, a total solar eclipse is predicted to last approximately 7 minutes and 29 seconds, making it the longest of the century by a wide margin.

title: There's a Tradition in Spain of Throwing Tomatoes at Each Other
fact: Each August, the town of Buñol hosts La Tomatina, a festival where tens of thousands of participants throw over 100 tons of ripe tomatoes at one another purely for fun.

title: Some Fish Can Climb Waterfalls Using Their Mouths
fact: Hawaii's native gobies, called o'opu, use suction cups formed by their pelvic and mouth structures to climb vertical waterfalls hundreds of feet high in order to reach freshwater streams.

title: There's a Language Where Every Sentence Must Indicate How the Speaker Knows the Information
fact: Turkish and several other languages use evidentiality markers, requiring speakers to grammatically specify whether they witnessed an event directly or heard about it secondhand.

title: There Was a Building Boom of Skyscrapers Race in 1930s New York That Was Kept Secret Until the Last Minute
fact: The Chrysler Building's architect secretly assembled a hidden spire inside the structure and raised it in a matter of minutes to surpass 40 Wall Street as the world's tallest building in 1930.

title: There's a Fish That Can Survive Out of Water for Days by Walking on Land
fact: The mudskipper can breathe through its skin and mouth lining, allowing it to leave water entirely and move across mudflats using its muscular pectoral fins for extended periods.

title: The World's Smallest Reptile Was Discovered on a Tiny Island in Madagascar
fact: Brookesia nana, a chameleon species discovered in 2021, measures under 22 millimeters long, small enough to fit comfortably on a human fingertip.

title: There's a Salt Flat So Flat It's Used to Calibrate Satellites
fact: Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni, the world's largest salt flat, is so extraordinarily level that space agencies use it as a reference surface to calibrate satellite altimeters.

title: A Piano Has More Possible Melodies Than Atoms in the Universe
fact: Because of the sheer number of possible note, rhythm, and duration combinations across a piano's 88 keys, mathematicians have noted the space of possible melodies vastly exceeds the estimated number of atoms in the observable universe.

title: There's a Species of Jellyfish with No Brain That Can Still Learn
fact: Box jellyfish lack a centralized brain but have been shown in studies to learn from visual experience, associating obstacles with turning behavior despite having only a distributed nerve net.

title: The Eiffel Tower Has a Secret Apartment at the Top
fact: Gustave Eiffel built a private apartment for himself near the tower's summit, which he used to host guests including Thomas Edison, and it remains preserved today.

title: There's a Type of Rain That Never Reaches the Ground
fact: Called virga, this phenomenon occurs when rain evaporates in dry air before hitting the surface, often visible as wispy streaks trailing beneath clouds in desert regions.

title: Some Ancient Roman Recipes Used Fermented Fish Sauce in Nearly Every Dish
fact: Garum, a pungent fermented fish sauce, was a staple condiment across the Roman Empire, added to everything from meats to desserts much like modern soy sauce or fish sauce today.

title: There's a Species of Bird That Builds the Largest Nests of Any Animal
fact: Sociable weaver birds in southern Africa construct massive communal nests that can house over a hundred breeding pairs and persist for generations, sometimes weighing over a ton.

title: The Word 'Sabotage' May Come from Workers Throwing Their Shoes into Machinery
fact: One popular etymology traces 'sabotage' to French laborers who allegedly threw wooden shoes called sabots into factory machines to disrupt production during disputes.

title: There's a Cave in Mexico Filled with Giant Crystals
fact: The Cave of the Crystals in Naica contains selenite beams up to 39 feet long, formed over hundreds of thousands of years in a uniquely stable, mineral-rich underground environment.

title: A Group of Pandas Is Called an Embarrassment
fact: Despite their solitary nature making group gatherings rare, the collective noun for a group of giant pandas is officially 'an embarrassment.'

title: There Was a 19th-Century Fad Where People Kept Pet Rocks as Fashionable Companions
fact: The famous 1975 Pet Rock craze wasn't the first of its kind; ornamental stones and curiosities were popular parlor novelties among Victorian households as conversation pieces.

title: The Sun Loses Millions of Tons of Mass Every Second
fact: Through nuclear fusion, the Sun converts roughly 4 million tons of matter into energy every second, though this is a negligible fraction of its total mass over its lifetime.

title: There's an Island Where Rabbits Vastly Outnumber People
fact: Okunoshima, a small Japanese island, is home to hundreds of wild rabbits believed to descend from animals released decades ago, drawing tourists who come to feed them.

title: Sharks Predate Saturn's Rings
fact: While Saturn's rings are estimated to be only around 100 million to a few hundred million years old, sharks have existed for roughly 400 million years, making them considerably older.

title: There's a Tribe of Bees That Makes Chocolate-Colored Honey
fact: Certain stingless bee species in tropical regions produce honey with unusually dark, complex flavors due to the specific plant nectars available in their rainforest habitats.

title: The First Alarm Clock Couldn't Be Set to Any Time Except 4 AM
fact: Levi Hutchins invented an early mechanical alarm clock in 1787 designed solely to wake him at 4 a.m. for his own personal schedule, with no adjustable settings.

title: There's a Type of Lizard That Can Run on Water
fact: The basilisk lizard, nicknamed the 'Jesus Christ lizard,' can sprint across water's surface by rapidly slapping its feet to create air pockets that briefly prevent it from sinking.

title: There's a Museum in Iceland Dedicated Entirely to Phallic Specimens
fact: The Icelandic Phallological Museum in Reykjavik houses preserved penis specimens from nearly every mammal species found in the country, including whales and even a claimed human sample.

title: A Cloud Forest Can Get Most of Its Water from Fog Rather Than Rain
fact: Tropical cloud forests, found at high altitudes, often rely on fine mist and fog condensing on leaves as their primary water source, rather than direct rainfall.

title: There's a Country Where It's Illegal to Not Vote
fact: Australia enforces compulsory voting, requiring eligible citizens to cast a ballot in federal elections or face a small fine, a policy in place since 1924.

title: The Praying Mantis Is the Only Insect That Can Turn Its Head 180 Degrees
fact: Unlike most insects, the praying mantis has a flexible neck joint allowing it to rotate its head nearly all the way around to track prey without moving its body.

title: There's a Waterfall in Venezuela So Tall the Water Evaporates Before Reaching the Ground
fact: Angel Falls, the world's tallest waterfall at 3,212 feet, has water that turns to mist partway down due to strong winds, meaning it rarely lands as a continuous stream.

title: There Was a Point in History When Tulip Bulbs Were Worth More Than Houses
fact: During the Dutch 'Tulip Mania' of the 1630s, some rare tulip bulbs sold for more than ten times a skilled craftsman's annual salary before the speculative market suddenly collapsed.

title: There's a Snail That Can Regrow Its Own Eyes
fact: Certain land snail species have remarkable regenerative abilities, allowing them to regrow lost eyestalks, and sometimes even parts of their brain, within weeks of injury.

title: The Number of Possible Chess Games Exceeds the Number of Atoms in the Observable Universe
fact: The Shannon number, an estimate of possible unique chess games, is around 10^120, far surpassing the roughly 10^80 atoms thought to exist in the observable universe.

title: There's a Species of Octopus That Can Walk on Two Legs
fact: The veined octopus has been observed curling six of its arms into a coconut-shell-like shape and 'walking' bipedally along the seafloor using the remaining two arms.

title: A Single Teaspoon of Soil Can Contain Billions of Microorganisms
fact: Healthy soil is teeming with life, with a single teaspoon estimated to hold anywhere from a few hundred million to several billion bacteria, along with fungi and other microbes.

title: There's a Bridge in China Made Entirely of Glass That Cracked on Its Opening Day
fact: The Yuntai Mountain glass bridge in Henan reportedly developed a crack from a dropped metal object on its opening day, causing brief panic despite being structurally reinforced and safe.

title: The Ancient Greeks Believed the Brain's Purpose Was to Cool the Blood
fact: Aristotle theorized that the heart, not the brain, was the seat of thought and emotion, believing instead that the brain functioned mainly as a radiator to cool overheated blood.

title: There's a Species of Ant Whose Queen Can Live for Nearly Three Decades
fact: Certain leafcutter ant queens have been recorded living up to 28 years in captivity, making them among the longest-lived insects ever documented.

title: There Was a Time When Coca-Cola Contained Actual Coca Leaf Extract
fact: The original 1886 Coca-Cola formula included small amounts of cocaine derived from coca leaves, which was removed from the recipe by 1929 as regulations tightened.

title: There's a Fish That Can Generate Electricity Strong Enough to Stun a Horse
fact: Electric eels can produce discharges of up to 600 volts, an amount capable of temporarily incapacitating a large animal like a horse in shallow water.

title: The Longest Recorded Game of Monopoly Lasted Over 70 Days
fact: According to Guinness World Records, the longest continuous Monopoly game on record lasted more than 1,680 hours, played by a group determined to set the mark.

title: There's a Species of Moth Whose Larvae Eat Nothing but Wool and Hair
fact: Clothes moth larvae possess enzymes capable of digesting keratin, allowing them to feed on wool, fur, and hair, making them notorious pests in closets and museums alike.

title: There's an Entire City Beneath Seattle from the 1889 Fire
fact: After a fire destroyed downtown Seattle, the city was rebuilt one story higher, leaving the original ground-level storefronts intact underground, now toured as the 'Seattle Underground.'

title: Some Species of Frogs Give Birth Through Their Backs
fact: The Suriname toad has skin on its back that forms pockets where fertilized eggs develop, with fully formed baby toads eventually emerging directly from the mother's back.

title: There's a Desert That Receives Snow Almost Every Year
fact: The Atacama Desert in Chile, one of the driest places on Earth, occasionally experiences rare snowfall at its higher elevations despite average annual rainfall of less than an inch.

title: The First Ever Webcam Was Built to Monitor a Coffee Pot
fact: Researchers at Cambridge University set up a camera in 1991 pointed at a coffee machine so they could check its status remotely without walking to another room, inspiring the first webcam feed.

title: There's a Species of Beetle That Can Survive Being Run Over by a Car
fact: The diabolical ironclad beetle has an exceptionally durable exoskeleton capable of withstanding forces exceeding 39,000 times its body weight, inspiring engineers studying impact-resistant materials.

title: There Was a Roman Emperor Who Reportedly Made His Horse a Senator
fact: Ancient historians recorded that Emperor Caligula threatened or intended to appoint his favorite horse, Incitatus, to the Roman Senate, though scholars debate whether this was ever fully carried out.

title: There's a Fruit That Makes Sour Foods Taste Sweet
fact: The miracle fruit contains a protein called miraculin that temporarily binds to taste buds, making sour foods like lemons taste remarkably sweet for up to an hour after consumption.

title: There's a Star Known to Be Cooler Than a Campfire
fact: Brown dwarfs, sometimes called 'failed stars,' can have surface temperatures as low as a few hundred degrees, with some discovered cool enough to be comparable to a household oven or campfire.

title: There's a Species of Shrimp That Can See Colors Humans Can't Even Imagine
fact: Mantis shrimp possess up to 16 types of color-receptive cones, compared to just three in humans, allowing them to perceive ultraviolet and polarized light beyond typical human perception.

title: There Was a Point When London's River Thames Was So Polluted It Was Declared Biologically Dead
fact: In 1957, the Natural History Museum officially declared the River Thames biologically dead due to severe pollution, though cleanup efforts since then have restored it to support over 100 fish species.

title: There's a Species of Gecko That Can Detach Its Skin to Escape Predators
fact: The fish-scale gecko has unusually delicate skin that tears away easily when grabbed, allowing it to slip free from a predator's grip and later regrow the lost skin.

title: There's a Mountain Range Hidden Entirely Beneath Antarctica's Ice
fact: The Gamburtsev Mountains, roughly the size of the European Alps, lie completely buried under Antarctic ice and were only mapped in detail using radar and satellite technology.

title: The Inventor of the Rubik's Cube Couldn't Solve It for a Month
fact: Hungarian professor Ernő Rubik took about a month to solve his own puzzle after inventing it in 1974, since he had built the mechanism before figuring out how to restore it.

title: There's a Species of Ant That Farms Fungus as Its Primary Food Source
fact: Leafcutter ants cultivate fungus gardens by feeding them chewed leaf fragments, forming a symbiotic agricultural relationship that has existed for tens of millions of years.

title: There's a Phenomenon Where the Sky Can Glow Green During Powerful Storms
fact: A rare optical effect sometimes seen before severe thunderstorms causes the sky to take on a greenish tint, believed to result from sunlight scattering through large hail-forming clouds.

title: There's a Tradition in Japan of Apologizing to Used Sewing Needles Before Discarding Them
fact: Hari-Kuyo is a Japanese ceremony where broken or worn sewing needles are respectfully laid to rest in soft tofu or gel, thanking them for their service before disposal.

title: There's a Bird That Mimics Chainsaws and Camera Shutters
fact: The Australian lyrebird is capable of imitating an extraordinary range of sounds, including man-made noises like chainsaws, car alarms, and camera shutters, in addition to other birds' calls.

title: There's an Entire Field of Study Dedicated to the Science of Tickling
fact: Gargalesis, the scientific term for the sensation of intense tickling, has been studied by neuroscientists trying to understand why humans can't effectively tickle themselves.

title: There's a Planet Where It Rains Glass Sideways
fact: On exoplanet HD 189733b, astronomers detected silicate particles in its atmosphere that form molten glass, driven sideways by winds estimated to reach 5,400 miles per hour.

title: There's a Moon in Our Solar System with More Volcanoes Than Any Other Body
fact: Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active object known, with hundreds of active volcanoes driven by intense tidal heating from Jupiter's gravitational pull.

title: Octopuses Can Taste Light Through Their Skin
fact: Research has found that octopus skin contains photoreceptors similar to those in the eye, potentially allowing them to sense light levels across their entire body.

title: There's a Star Cluster Where the Sky Would Never Get Fully Dark
fact: In the dense core of a globular cluster like Omega Centauri, thousands of stars packed closely together would make the night sky glow almost as bright as dusk from any orbiting planet.

title: There's an Ancient Roman Road Still in Use Today
fact: Via Appia, built starting in 312 BCE to connect Rome to southern Italy, remains partially walkable and drivable in some stretches over 2,300 years after its construction.

title: There's a Species of Woodpecker That Can Peck Trees 20 Times a Second
fact: Woodpeckers can strike wood at speeds of up to 20 pecks per second, absorbing shock forces that would cause a concussion in humans thanks to specialized skull structures.

title: There's a Star That Explodes Repeatedly Instead of Just Once
fact: Recurrent novae, like the star system T Coronae Borealis, undergo periodic thermonuclear explosions on their surface every few decades without being fully destroyed each time.
